notes.meaning: The Benjamites marched out of Gibeah and killed another eighteen thousand Israelite soldiers on this second day of fighting. This brought Israel's two-day losses to forty thousand men, even though their cause against evil was right. God allowed this heavy loss to humble the nation, showing them that doing the right thing still requires deep personal humility before Him.

The entire assembly went up to Bethel, weeping and sitting before the Lord until evening without eating. Fasting meant giving up food for a time to show genuine sorrow for their sins, while burnt offerings and peace offerings sought God's pardon and restored fellowship. Israel finally understood that they needed to repent of their own sins rather than trusting in their large numbers.

The Israelites asked the Lord whether they should attack their brother tribe again or end the war entirely. Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, ministered as high priest before the ark of the covenant, which had been brought temporarily to Bethel. Because the people now asked in genuine humility and yielded entirely to God's will, the Lord promised to give them complete victory the next day.

Even though God promised them victory, the Israelites did not become careless, but planned a wise military ambush around Gibeah. They stationed hidden soldiers near the town while preparing the main army to draw the enemy out. This plan matched the tactics Joshua used at the battle of Ai.

On the third day of battle, the Israelites marched up to Gibeah and lined up for battle just as they had done before. This open movement was meant to look like their previous attacks so the Benjamites would expect another easy victory.

Benjamin charged out of the city gates and began striking down Israelite soldiers along the open roads toward Bethel and Gibeah. Israel pretended to flee in panic, losing about thirty men during the retreat. Benjamin assumed they were winning as easily as before, unaware that Israel was luring them away from their city defenses.

The main army of Israel stopped their staged retreat and formed battle lines at a place called Baal-tamar. At the same time, the hidden Israelite troops burst out from their positions west of Gibeah. This coordinated move caught the Benjamite forces between two armies.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this chapter as a combination of two older accounts and regard parts of this verse as an early addition to the text.

notes.meaning: Ten thousand chosen Israelite troops launched a direct assault against Gibeah, and the fighting grew extremely fierce. The Benjamites fought hard, but they did not know that disaster was closing in on them. Their overconfidence blinded them to the trap that had been set.

The Lord gave Israel the victory, and more than twenty-five thousand Benjamite soldiers were killed that day. The writer emphasizes that God Himself defeated Benjamin, fulfilling the promise He gave at Bethel. This verse summarizes the total outcome before the next verses describe the details of the fight.
The soldiers of Benjamin finally saw that they were losing the battle. Israel had given ground earlier only because they were depending on the ambush waiting near the town.
The hidden Israelite troops rushed suddenly into Gibeah while it was left unguarded. They spread throughout the city and put all its remaining inhabitants to death.

The army had agreed on a clear signal: the ambush was to set the city on fire so a massive cloud of smoke would rise into the air. While Benjamin was cutting down about thirty Israelites and celebrating another supposed victory, the smoke began to rise. That signal told the retreating Israelite troops to turn around and counterattack.
A thick column of smoke began rising high into the sky from the city. When the Benjamite soldiers looked back over their shoulders, they were stunned to see their entire city burning in flames.
The retreating Israelites suddenly stopped, turned around, and charged the enemy. The men of Benjamin panicked when they saw their home destroyed and realized total ruin had caught up with them.
The Benjamites broke ranks and tried to escape toward the wilderness. The battle swept after them, and Israelite troops from the nearby towns joined the pursuit and cut them down in the open.
Israelite soldiers closed in on the fleeing Benjamites from all sides, giving them no place to rest or regroup. They chased them relentlessly and easily ran them down east of Gibeah.

Eighteen thousand brave Benjamite soldiers died during the primary battle and the first retreat. Even though they were courageous and skilled warriors, their bravery could not rescue them from God's judgment.

The survivors turned and ran toward a rocky hill known as the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites hunted down five thousand more along the main roads and struck down another two thousand near Gidom, leaving almost no one behind.

A total of twenty-five thousand Benjamite swordsmen fell that day, all of them courageous soldiers. This rounded total sums up the losses on the third day of fighting, showing that nearly the entire army had been wiped out.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that verses 45 and 46 were added later by an editor who calculated the total from the numbers in the narrative.

notes.meaning: Only six hundred Benjamite men managed to escape to the rugged caves of the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed for four months. By sheltering this small group in a mountain stronghold, God kept the tribe of Benjamin from being completely erased.

The Israelites turned back into the territory of Benjamin and destroyed every town they reached, killing the defenseless people, slaughtering the livestock, and setting everything on fire. In their uncontrolled rage, they took their vengeance to a tragic extreme by wiping out whole families.
